title: Links and Navigation
subtitle: Connect pages and help users find their way
description: Learn how hyperlinks work, how to connect local pages, link to external websites, navigate within a page, and write useful accessible links.

blocks.text: Welcome! Let's connect the web

Welcome back! In Lesson 1, you learned how HTML structures a webpage. In Lesson 2, you learned how to organise text with headings, paragraphs, and emphasis. Now imagine a website containing ten pages, but no way to move from one page to another. Visitors would have to know every address and enter it manually. Hyperlinks solve this problem by connecting documents and resources so users can navigate naturally.

You use links every day when you open a help article, follow a reference, visit another page, or jump to a section of a long document. In HTML, the anchor element, written as a, creates a hyperlink. Its href attribute specifies the destination. In this lesson, you will build links to other websites, connect pages in the same project, create links to specific sections, and learn how to make link text understandable. By the end, you will be able to plan simple navigation for a real website.
Section 1 — Understanding the anchor element

The anchor element is written with an opening tag, link text, and a closing tag. A basic link looks like Visit Example. The words Visit Example are the text users can see and select. The href attribute contains the destination. If you leave out href, the anchor does not behave as a normal destination link. Remember the distinction: a is the element, href is the attribute, and Visit Example is the visible link text.

A hyperlink can point to an external website, a different file in your project, a section of the current page, an email address, or another supported destination. The destination format tells the browser what kind of navigation is intended. For an external website, use its URL. For a local page, use the file path. For a location within the same page, use a fragment identifier beginning with a hash sign. You will practise each type separately so that the differences become clear.

Link text matters. If every link says Click here, users may struggle to understand where each one leads, especially when using assistive technology or scanning a page quickly. Text such as Read the HTML documentation or Open the course outline explains the destination more clearly. A link should make sense in its surrounding context and, where possible, even when read on its own. This is a small decision that makes a website easier to use.

blocks.text: Preview the example and select the link if your preview environment allows navigation. Notice that the href contains the complete destination, while the words between the tags describe the link. A browser normally navigates to the destination when the user activates it. blocks.question: You are building a course page and want the words 'Open the CSS guide' to lead to a specific website. Which implementation correctly defines both the visible text and its destination?
blocks.explanation: The anchor element creates the link, and href specifies its destination. The link text sits between the opening and closing anchor tags. src is commonly used for embedded resources such as images, not as the anchor's destination attribute.
blocks.hint: Which attribute belongs on an anchor element to specify where it navigates?

blocks.text: Section 2 — Connect pages inside your project

Most websites contain multiple pages. A learning platform might have index.html for its home page, courses.html for its course list, and contact.html for its contact information. If these files are in the same directory, a link can refer to another file using its filename. For example, Browse courses points to courses.html relative to the current document's location. This is called a relative URL because the destination is interpreted in relation to the current page.

File organisation affects relative links. Suppose your project contains index.html and a folder named lessons, with html-basics.html inside that folder. From index.html, the relative path is lessons/html-basics.html. From html-basics.html, a link back to index.html would commonly use ../index.html because the two-dot path segment moves up one directory. A path that works from one file may not work from another because each relative path is resolved from the current document's URL.

A common mistake is writing a filename or folder path that does not match the actual project. A link can look perfectly valid but lead to a missing page because the filename is misspelled, the folder is different, or the file was never uploaded. Depending on the hosting environment, uppercase and lowercase letters may also matter. Check the actual folder structure and spelling when a local link fails. Do not assume every broken link is caused by the anchor syntax itself.

You can use absolute URLs or relative URLs for local navigation, but each serves a different purpose. An absolute URL includes the full address, such as https://example.com/courses.html. A relative URL might simply be courses.html or lessons/html-basics.html. Relative paths are useful when a project is moved to a different domain because the internal links can continue to work as long as the file structure remains the same. Choose the path that matches the way your project is organised.

blocks.code: Home Courses HTML Basics Contact
blocks.output: A navigation region with four links. Each destination must exist at the specified relative path for navigation to succeed.

blocks.text: The nav element identifies a group of navigation links. The aria-label attribute gives this navigation region a descriptive name for assistive technologies. This example does not automatically create the destination pages; it only provides links to them. If you copy the example into a project, create the referenced files or adjust the href values to match your existing files. Semantic structure and correct paths work together to create useful navigation.

blocks.question: Your project has this structure: index.html and a folder named lessons containing basics.html. You are writing a link inside index.html to open basics.html. Which href is the correct relative path?
blocks.explanation: The lessons folder is located beside index.html, so the relative path from index.html is lessons/basics.html. The ../ segment would move up a directory before looking for lessons, which is not needed in this structure.
blocks.hint: Start from the directory containing index.html, then enter the lessons folder.

blocks.text: Section 3 — Jump to a specific section

Some pages are long enough that users need to jump directly to a particular section. HTML supports fragment links for this purpose. First, assign an id to the destination element. Then create a link whose href contains a hash followed by that id. For example, an element with id="pricing" can be targeted by a link written as View pricing. When the link is activated, the browser attempts to navigate to that element within the current document.

An id should identify one element in a document and should be unique within that document. If several elements share the same id, fragment navigation may not target the element you intended, and scripts or styles that rely on the id can become confusing. Choose a descriptive id, such as course-outline or contact-details, and use the same spelling in the link's fragment. The hash sign belongs in the href fragment, not in the id attribute value itself.

Fragment links can also target an element on another page. For example, courses.html#python can open courses.html and navigate to the element whose id is python. This is useful when a course directory contains many sections and you want to link directly to one of them. The destination page must actually contain that id. If the id is absent or misspelled, the browser may open the page without jumping to the intended section.

A table of contents often uses fragment links to connect each topic name to a section further down the page. This gives readers control over where they begin reading. When building a long tutorial, use meaningful headings and unique ids so that the page can be navigated easily. You can also use fragment links to support sharing a direct reference to a particular section, rather than forcing visitors to search through the whole document.

blocks.output: A course guide with three links that jump to the matching sections on the same page.

blocks.text: Test the table of contents in a browser. Select Resources and notice how the page moves to that section when there is enough content for scrolling. In a short preview, the section may already be visible, so the movement can be subtle. The important connection is the matching pair: href="#resources" targets id="resources". If the spelling differs, the intended target cannot be identified correctly.

blocks.question: A link uses href="#account", but clicking it does not jump to the account section. Which change is the most direct correction if the intended section currently has no id?
options: Add id="account" to the intended destination element.
Add href="#account" to every paragraph on the page.
Change the destination element's class to account without changing its id.
Place the hash sign inside the text of the destination heading.
blocks.explanation: A fragment link targets an element by its id. Adding id="account" to the intended destination gives href="#account" a matching target. A class name alone does not serve as the target for an ordinary fragment link.
blocks.hint: Match the fragment after the hash to the destination element's id.

blocks.text: Section 4 — External links, new tabs, and useful destinations

An external link points to a resource outside your own site. Its href normally includes a URL such as https://developer.mozilla.org/. A complete URL often begins with a scheme such as https, followed by the host name and optionally a path. Using a complete external URL makes the intended destination explicit. Prefer secure HTTPS addresses when the destination supports them, and check that the address points to the resource you intend to recommend.

By default, a link usually navigates in the current browsing context. If you want a link to request a new tab or window, you can use target="_blank". However, opening a new tab should be a deliberate decision, because unexpected navigation can confuse users, particularly on mobile devices. Explain the destination clearly and do not force every link into a new tab. Users should be able to understand where a link leads before activating it.

When using target="_blank", adding rel="noopener" is a good defensive practice. It prevents the newly opened page from receiving access to the opening page through the window.opener reference in supporting browsers. Modern browsers generally provide this protection automatically for target blank links, but writing rel="noopener" makes your intent explicit. You may also see rel="noreferrer", which additionally suppresses the referrer information sent with the request. Use these attributes when their behavior fits your privacy and security needs.

Links can point to more than web pages. A mailto link can open a user's configured email application with a recipient address, such as mailto:help@example.com. A telephone link can use tel:+233200000000 on supported devices. These links do not send an email or place a call by themselves; they ask the device to open an appropriate handler. Always use a valid destination and make the visible link text explain the action.

blocks.title: Sample 4 — External, email, and telephone links
blocks.code:
Get More Help

Read the HTML reference

Email the support team

Call the support line
blocks.output: A page with a documentation link, an email link, and a telephone link. Email and phone links depend on compatible apps or device handlers.

blocks.text: The example uses a demonstration email address and telephone number. Replace them with valid destinations before using this pattern on a real website. Do not publish someone else's contact details without permission. Also remember that an external link can be syntactically correct and still lead to an unavailable page, a changed resource, or an untrusted website. Test destinations and choose sources carefully, especially when recommending them to students.

blocks.question: You want an external documentation link to open in a new tab and explicitly prevent the new page from accessing the opening page through window.opener. Which implementation best expresses that intention?
blocks.explanation: The href attribute provides the destination, target="_blank" requests a new browsing context, and rel="noopener" explicitly prevents the opened page from accessing the opener reference. The other choices misuse attributes or select the current browsing context.
blocks.hint: Check the destination attribute, the new-tab target, and the security-related rel value.

blocks.text: Section 5 — Accessible links and debugging navigation

A link should be understandable to different users, including people who navigate with a keyboard or screen reader. Use descriptive text such as Download the HTML practice sheet instead of repeating Click here for every destination. Make sure links can be identified visually and that keyboard users can reach and activate them. Browsers usually provide keyboard support for ordinary anchor elements when they have a valid href, so using the correct HTML element gives you useful behavior without writing JavaScript.

Avoid using an anchor as a substitute for a button when the purpose is to perform an action rather than navigate to a destination. A link takes a user somewhere; a button normally performs an action on the current page, such as submitting a form or opening a dialog. The two can look similar after styling, but their purposes differ. Choosing the right element helps assistive technologies communicate what users can expect.

When a link fails, check the actual href value first. For a local file, confirm the relative path and filename. For a fragment link, verify that the target id exists and matches exactly. For an external link, inspect the full URL and test whether the destination is available. Also check that another element is not covering the link or that the preview environment is not restricting navigation. Diagnose one possible cause at a time instead of changing unrelated markup.

Let's connect the ideas to a practical project. Create a home page with links to Courses, About, and Contact. Put each destination in its own file, or update the href values to match the pages you already have. On a long course page, add a small table of contents with fragment links. Give each link descriptive text, test every destination, and check the page using keyboard navigation. These steps turn isolated anchors into a useful navigation system.

One final habit will help you become a better developer: do not assume that a link is correct just because it looks clickable. Confirm that its destination matches its visible description, that it behaves as expected, and that users can understand its purpose. A link to a Python lesson should not accidentally open a CSS lesson. In a real project, systematic testing prevents small path mistakes from becoming frustrating navigation problems.

blocks.question: A course dashboard displays a link labelled 'Open Python Lesson 1', but its href points to css_lesson_1.json. The link opens a file, yet the destination is wrong. What is the best correction?
options: Keep the destination and change the label to 'Open Python Lesson 1' in bold.
Remove href and use a class named python so the browser chooses the correct file.
Add target="_blank" because opening a new tab fixes the incorrect destination.
Change href to the correct Python lesson destination and verify that the referenced file exists.
blocks.explanation: The destination must match the link's intended purpose. Changing visual styling or opening a new tab does not correct a wrong path. Update href to the correct destination and confirm that the target exists and can be opened by the application.
blocks.hint: The visible label and the actual destination must refer to the same lesson.

blocks.text: Lesson recap — You can now connect pages

Excellent work! You have learned how the anchor element and href attribute create hyperlinks, how relative paths connect files inside a project, and how fragment links jump to specific sections. You have also explored external links, new-tab behavior, email and telephone links, descriptive link text, and practical ways to debug broken destinations. These skills are essential for navigation menus, course dashboards, documentation sites, and nearly every multi-page website.

Before continuing, build a small navigation page with three local links and one external reference. Then create a long page with two sections and use fragment links to jump between them. Test every link and deliberately introduce one incorrect path so you can practise diagnosing the problem. In Lesson 4, you will learn how to add images and choose appropriate attributes so visual content appears correctly and remains understandable to users who cannot see it.
